newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe rules out early elections.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe rules out early elections.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Sunday ruled out an early election or a cabinet reshuffle despite plummeting popularity and coalition infighting, saying his policies would yield results in coming months.
Polls show the centre-right premier's popularity has fallen to an all-time low against a backdrop of near-record unemployment and criticism from inside his ruling centre-right coalition.
"I see no reason for early elections," Juppe told TF1 television in an interview.

President Jacques Chirac, he said, could dissolve parliament earlier than the scheduled early 1998 deadline only if the National Assembly (lower house) overthrew the government or if there was "an open crisis".
"That's not the case today. A dissolution after a vote of confidence in the National Assembly has no meaning," Juppe said.
He said his ministerial team was "very good" and asked: "Why change a team which believes in what it is doing and whose policies, I believe, will yield results?".
He said France's economic recovery was solid, and that growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) would accelerate next year beyond this year's forecast 1.3 percent.

In an interview published on Saturday by the pro-government Le Figaro, sacked finance minister Alain Madelin warned that if the government did not succeed in curing economic woes "the situation could become dangerous given the gap between those who govern and those who are governed".
"On many issues," the outspoken free-marketeer added, "I have ideas which are often very different from Juppe's...To win (1998) general elections, we must win the battle for jobs."

Madelin and former Interior Minister Charles Pasqua among others have criticised Juppe's austerity drive, prompting him to call a vote of confidence which he won on Wednesday in an attempt to rally the ruling centre-right coalition.

A Sofres survey for the weekly Le Figaro Magazine showed on Friday that just 27 percent of those questioned had confidence in conservative Juppe in late September against 34 a month earlier. The numbers lacking confidence rose to 71 percent from 69.
